title: Quick to hear (James 1:19–27)
hook: swift to hear, slow to speak; pure religion visits orphans and widows
carry: swift to hear, slow to speak

segments.voice: Yesterday, every good gift, and your line was from the father of lights. Which gift did you name under the sky last night? Day six hundred seventy-one.

You're telling a friend something that matters. Halfway through, you can see it: they've stopped listening. Their eyes have that look. They're loading their reply. The second you take a breath, out it comes, about them. Everybody has been on both sides of that. James has three short rules for it, and they're some of the most quoted words in his letter. Then, a few lines later, he holds up a mirror, and finally he gives his own definition of what religion is for. It's not the definition most people would guess.

In the King James Bible: "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Fast ears. Slow mouth. Slower temper. The order matters: if you're quick to hear, you're less likely to need the other two. James says anger doesn't produce the kind of goodness God wants. Then he turns from listening to people to listening to God's word, and he pushes one step further. "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." Hearing is not the finish line. And here's his picture. Someone looks at their face in a mirror, sees it plainly, walks away, and "straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was." In his day mirrors were polished metal, and the image was dim. Still, you saw enough. Spinach in your teeth. Hair sticking up. And then you walk off and forget. James says that's hearing without doing. You saw it, and nothing changed. Then his definition: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world." Look what's on that list. Not a building. Not a feeling. Two things. Show up for the people with no one to protect them: in his world, orphans and widows had no income and no voice. And keep yourself clean. Care outward, integrity inward. The word for religion here means outward worship, the practice people could see. James is saying: if you want to see someone's religion, watch where they go on a Tuesday afternoon.
screen: then, large: `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen more than you talk. Settle, and breathe. For the first minute, just listen. Not to your thoughts. To the room. Every sound: a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breathing, a voice in another room. Try to catch the farthest sound and the nearest. Notice how often your mind wants to comment on what it hears, to name it or judge it. Let the comments go and keep listening. Then think of one person you'll talk with today, and decide to let them finish every sentence. If you pray, you can ask for quick ears. The bell holds the time.
Quick to hear. James's rule for every conversation: swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger, and then do what you heard.
Your line: swift to hear, slow to speak. In your next real conversation, count one slow breath after the other person stops before you answer. Day six hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Many Christian communities take James 1:27 as a charter for practical care, and churches run visiting ministries, food pantries and foster-care support with this verse in mind.

fork.setup: you've just looked in the mirror and seen something wrong. what does James say most hearers do?
options: walk off and forget what they saw.

original.note: Greek: religion as outward worship, the practice others can see. James gives it a practical definition.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite rule about manners.
what it means: listening first, speaking later, and doing what you hear: caring for those with no protector.
what a scholar hears: thrēskeia, outward religious practice, redefined by James as visiting orphans and widows, the most vulnerable people in his world.

θρησκεία (1:26–27) as outward religious observance: standard lexical gloss. Confirm.
